displayPolicy: Featured entries have fuller copy; expanded gallery is spoiler-conscious. H entries are editorial placeholders held out of before-reading display. Initial Pride and Prejudice and Odyssey cards were accepted by Anders in this review; other prose remains for review. Line counts vary with viewport.

characters.name: Victor Frankenstein
characters.body: Victor leaves his family in Geneva to study the workings of nature at Ingolstadt. Brilliant, ambitious and increasingly absorbed in his research, he dreams of discovering how life begins. He tells the central story of the novel, inviting us to see both his achievement and its consequences through his eyes.

characters.name: The creature
characters.body: Brought to life and immediately abandoned, the creature must discover the world without a parent or a guide. He is curious, sensitive and eager to learn, but his appearance frightens the people he approaches. His longing for affection and a place among others gives him questions his creator would rather avoid.

characters.name: Robert Walton
characters.role: The explorer whose letters open the novel
characters.body: An English captain seeking a passage through the Arctic. In letters to his sister, he describes his hopes for discovery and his loneliness. When he takes a stranger aboard, he becomes the listener through whom we first hear Victor's story.

characters.name: Margaret Saville
characters.body: The recipient of Walton's letters in England. Her brother writes to her for understanding and reassurance across the distance between home and his expedition.

characters.name: Alphonse Frankenstein
characters.body: A respected citizen of Geneva, devoted to his family and concerned for Victor's future. His letters keep calling his absent son back towards home.

characters.name: Caroline Frankenstein, née Beaufort
characters.body: A compassionate presence in Victor's account of his childhood. Her care for vulnerable people helps establish the family world he remembers.

characters.name: Elizabeth Lavenza
characters.body: Raised with Victor in the Frankenstein household. Her affection and attachment to family life provide a measure of what his solitary ambitions draw him away from.

characters.name: Henry Clerval
characters.body: A warm, imaginative young man from Geneva, drawn to stories, languages and adventure. He brings friendship into Victor's increasingly solitary life.

characters.name: William Frankenstein
characters.body: The youngest child in the Frankenstein household, much loved by the family. He belongs to the domestic world Victor leaves behind.

characters.name: Ernest Frankenstein
characters.body: The middle Frankenstein son. News of his interests and future appears in the family's accounts of life in Geneva.

characters.name: Justine Moritz
characters.role: A young woman close to the family
characters.body: Taken into the Frankenstein household when young and treated with affection. She works within the family and is especially close to its children.

characters.name: De Lacey
characters.body: A blind older man living with his children in reduced circumstances. The ordinary affection of this household becomes important to the creature's understanding of human life.

characters.name: Felix De Lacey
characters.body: A young man who works to support his family. His labour, grief and tenderness gradually become legible to an observer outside the cottage.

characters.name: Agatha De Lacey
characters.body: She shares the work of the cottage and cares for her father. Her daily kindness is part of the family life the creature watches.

characters.name: Safie
characters.role: A visitor to the De Lacey household
characters.body: A young woman who arrives seeking Felix. As she learns the household's language, her lessons create another opportunity for someone nearby to learn.

characters.name: M. Krempe
characters.body: A professor of natural philosophy who dismisses Victor's enthusiasm for old alchemical writers and urges him towards contemporary science.

characters.name: M. Waldman
characters.body: A professor of chemistry whose generous account of scientific discovery excites Victor. His encouragement helps turn private fascination into sustained study.

characters.name: Elizabeth Bennet
characters.role: The second Bennet sister, also called Lizzy
characters.body: Quick-witted and observant, Elizabeth takes pleasure in the absurdities of the people around her. She wants affection in marriage and is reluctant to let money or rank decide whom she should admire. Her confidence in her own judgment makes every encounter with the reserved Mr. Darcy particularly interesting.

characters.name: Fitzwilliam Darcy
characters.body: Darcy arrives in the neighbourhood with his friend Charles Bingley, bringing a large fortune and little enthusiasm for making himself agreeable. His reserve can look like contempt, and his first encounter with Elizabeth gives her little reason to like him. He is accustomed to the privileges and expectations of his position.

characters.name: Jane Bennet
characters.body: Gentle, affectionate and slow to think badly of anyone, Jane sees reasons to hope where Elizabeth sees reasons to doubt. The sisters are close, despite their different ways of judging people. Jane's growing interest in Charles Bingley gives the Bennet household much to discuss.

characters.name: Charles Bingley
characters.body: A wealthy young man newly settled at Netherfield. His openness and good humour make him an immediate favourite in the neighbourhood.

characters.name: Mrs. Bennet
characters.body: Determined to see her five daughters married. Her noisy schemes can be embarrassing, but the family's uncertain financial future gives her genuine reasons to worry.

characters.name: Mr. Bennet
characters.body: The owner of Longbourn, happiest among his books. His dry humour delights Elizabeth, though amusement is often easier for him than involvement.

characters.name: Mary Bennet
characters.body: Earnest, studious and eager to display her accomplishments. She often brings a moral reflection to conversations her sisters approach less solemnly.

characters.name: Catherine “Kitty” Bennet
characters.body: Easily caught up in her younger sister Lydia's enthusiasms, especially for officers, outings and the excitement of company.

characters.name: Lydia Bennet
characters.body: High-spirited, confident and absorbed in officers and social pleasures. She pursues excitement with little patience for restraint.

characters.name: George Wickham
characters.body: An easy conversationalist whose manners make a strong impression on Elizabeth. He has a history with Darcy and his own account of their relationship.

characters.name: William Collins
characters.role: The cousin who will inherit Longbourn
characters.body: A clergyman with elaborate manners and a powerful patron. His position as the estate's future heir gives his visit particular significance.

characters.name: Charlotte Lucas
characters.body: Intelligent and clear-eyed about the choices available to a woman with little money. She and Elizabeth do not always want the same things from marriage.

characters.name: Lady Catherine de Bourgh
characters.body: A wealthy aristocrat who expects her opinions to carry authority in other people's lives. Mr. Collins depends on her patronage.

characters.name: Georgiana Darcy
characters.body: A shy young woman under her brother's protection. Other people's expectations often arrive before she has a chance to speak for herself.

characters.name: Caroline Bingley
characters.body: Attentive to rank, manners and Darcy's approval. Her politeness does not always make a visitor feel welcome.

characters.name: Mr. and Mrs. Gardiner
characters.role: The Bennet sisters' aunt and uncle
characters.body: Relatives living in London who offer affection, good sense and a wider perspective on the family's concerns.

characters.name: Sir William Lucas
characters.body: A neighbour fond of ceremony and distinguished company. He takes pleasure in bringing people together and recalling his own honours.

characters.name: Mr. and Mrs. Hurst
characters.role: Bingley's sister Louisa and her husband
characters.body: Members of the Netherfield party. Louisa shares Caroline's concern with social standing; her husband is principally interested in his own comfort.

characters.name: Anne de Bourgh
characters.body: A quiet, delicate young woman whose mother's expectations leave little room for anyone else to imagine her future.

characters.name: Odysseus
characters.body: A veteran of the Trojan War, renowned for ingenuity, endurance and a gift for making words serve him. He has been away from Ithaca for twenty years. His longing for home drives the poem, but his appetite for knowledge and recognition makes him a complicated man to follow.

characters.name: Penelope
characters.body: Odysseus's wife must live with uncertainty while suitors press her to remarry and consume her household's wealth. She has little force at her disposal, but considerable intelligence. Her skill in delaying, testing and interpreting other people makes the struggle at home as demanding as the journey across the sea.

characters.name: Telemachus
characters.role: A son growing up without his father
characters.body: Still a baby when Odysseus left for Troy, Telemachus has grown up inside the space his father left. He is angry at the suitors but uncertain of his own authority. The poem begins with his effort to discover what has happened to Odysseus and what he might do himself.

characters.name: Athena
characters.role: Goddess of wisdom and Odysseus's ally
characters.body: She takes an active interest in Odysseus and his household, often approaching mortals in disguise and encouraging them to act.

characters.name: Poseidon
characters.body: A powerful opponent of Odysseus. His anger makes the sea a place where human ingenuity and divine power meet.

characters.name: Zeus
characters.body: Presides over the divine assembly and weighs requests concerning mortal lives. Questions of justice and hospitality fall within his authority.

characters.name: Hermes
characters.body: Travels between divine and human worlds, carrying instructions and sometimes supplying practical help to a traveller in danger.

characters.name: Calypso
characters.role: The goddess keeping Odysseus on her island
characters.body: Wants Odysseus to remain with her and offers him immortality. Her beautiful island is also the place from which he longs to leave.

characters.name: The suitors
characters.body: A crowd of would-be husbands occupying Odysseus's household. Their demands put Penelope and Telemachus under increasing pressure.

characters.name: Antinous
characters.role: A forceful leader among the suitors
characters.body: Openly contemptuous of Telemachus and quick to assert the suitors' interests. His confidence makes him a conspicuous presence in the hall.

characters.name: Eurymachus
characters.body: More conciliatory in manner than Antinous, skilled at making reassuring speeches while pursuing his own position.

characters.name: Eurycleia
characters.body: An enslaved woman who has served the household for many years and helped raise both Odysseus and Telemachus.

characters.name: Eumaeus
characters.body: An enslaved member of the household living away from the palace. His conduct offers another view of loyalty and hospitality.

characters.name: Laertes
characters.body: Lives apart from the palace, weighed down by his son's absence. He represents another part of the home Odysseus hopes to recover.

characters.name: Nestor
characters.body: A survivor of the Trojan War, known for experience and counsel. Telemachus seeks news from him.

characters.name: Menelaus
characters.body: Helen's husband and a veteran of Troy. His own difficult return gives him news and memories to share with Telemachus.

characters.name: Helen
characters.body: Her departure for Troy stands behind the war. She tells her own stories of its people and events.

characters.name: Nausicaa
characters.body: The daughter of Alcinous and Arete. Her encounter with an unfamiliar traveller raises questions of kindness, reputation and welcome.

characters.name: Alcinous
characters.body: Rules a people renowned for their ships. A stranger arriving at his court must find a way to obtain a hearing.

characters.name: Arete
characters.body: A respected presence in the royal household, whose judgment matters to anyone hoping to be welcomed there.

characters.name: Circe
characters.body: A powerful and unsettling host encountered in Odysseus's account of his travels. Her island tests a visitor's caution.

characters.name: Polyphemus
characters.body: A giant living beyond the ordinary rules of hospitality. Odysseus recounts an encounter that pits force against ingenuity.

characters.name: Aeolus
characters.body: A ruler whose unusual authority over the weather offers a traveller the possibility of help.

characters.name: Helios
characters.body: His cattle are sacred. Respect for divine limits becomes a practical concern for hungry travellers.

characters.name: Tiresias
characters.body: A seer whose knowledge reaches beyond ordinary human understanding. Odysseus seeks guidance associated with him.

characters.name: Agamemnon
characters.role: Commander of the Greek army at Troy
characters.body: His household and return from war are repeatedly invoked as a troubling comparison with Odysseus's own.

characters.name: Achilles
characters.role: The great Greek warrior at Troy
characters.body: A central figure in memories of the war. His fame raises questions about the value and cost of a heroic life.

characters.name: Melanthius
characters.body: A servant whose conduct towards the suitors and visitors helps reveal how power has shifted during Odysseus's absence.

characters.name: Rodion Raskolnikov
characters.role: An impoverished former student, also called Rodya
characters.body: Proud, intelligent and increasingly isolated, Raskolnikov lives in a cramped room in St Petersburg. He moves between sudden generosity and contempt for the people around him. A theory about exceptional individuals has become intensely personal: he wants to know whether he is one of those entitled to cross ordinary moral boundaries.

characters.name: Sofya “Sonya” Marmeladova
characters.body: A young woman driven into prostitution to support her impoverished family. Sonya is shy and devout, living under judgments that overlook what she has endured for others. Her presence brings Raskolnikov into contact with a way of understanding suffering, responsibility and human worth very different from his own.

characters.name: Porfiry Petrovich
characters.body: An intelligent official with a disconcertingly informal manner. He takes an interest in ideas as well as evidence, and can make a conversation feel casual while leaving his listener unsure what has been noticed. His encounters with Raskolnikov turn questions of conscience into an immediate contest of attention.

characters.name: Dmitri Razumikhin
characters.body: Warm, energetic and practical, he keeps finding ways to help. His friendship meets Raskolnikov's isolation with stubborn involvement.

characters.name: Avdotya “Dunya” Raskolnikova
characters.body: Proud, capable and concerned for her family's future. Her plans for marriage bring money, sacrifice and independence into conflict.

characters.name: Pulcheria Alexandrovna
characters.body: Loving and anxious, she invests enormous hope in her children. Her letters carry both reassurance and the weight of expectation.

characters.name: Semyon Marmeladov
characters.body: A former clerk whose drinking has deepened his family's poverty. He speaks with painful eloquence about shame and the need for mercy.

characters.name: Katerina Ivanovna
characters.body: Ill, proud and struggling to care for children in desperate circumstances. Memories of a different social position intensify her humiliation.

characters.name: Pyotr Luzhin
characters.body: A prosperous man who presents marriage as an act of generosity. He has definite ideas about what gratitude should require.

characters.name: Arkady Svidrigailov
characters.body: A wealthy landowner whose interest in Dunya troubles her family. His easy manner leaves his intentions difficult to read.

characters.name: Alyona Ivanovna
characters.body: An older woman to whom Raskolnikov brings possessions for money. His thoughts increasingly turn her into an object in his private argument.

characters.name: Lizaveta Ivanovna
characters.body: A gentle, overworked woman accustomed to being ordered about. Her relationship with Alyona reveals another life within the same household.

characters.name: Nastasya
characters.body: Direct and practical, she brings food, conversation and occasional kindness into his increasingly disordered routine.

characters.name: Alexander Zametov
characters.body: A young official whose conversations with Raskolnikov take on more significance than their casual setting suggests.

characters.name: Andrei Lebezyatnikov
characters.body: Enthusiastic about progressive ideas and communal arrangements. His talk offers one of the novel's more comic encounters with fashionable theories.

characters.name: Niccolò Machiavelli
characters.role: The author seeking a return to public life
characters.body: A former official of the Florentine republic, writing after the loss of his position. He offers a ruler knowledge gathered from diplomacy and ancient history, while hoping to make himself useful again. Keep both the political observer and the man seeking employment in view as you read.

characters.name: Cesare Borgia
characters.body: The son of Pope Alexander VI, building a state in central Italy through force, alliances and calculated displays of power. Machiavelli uses his actions to examine how a new ruler establishes authority. His example also raises a difficult question about how far preparation can protect anyone from changes of fortune.

characters.name: Lorenzo de' Medici
characters.body: A younger member of the Medici family, to whom the surviving dedication addresses the book. He is not Lorenzo the Magnificent, who died in 1492. Machiavelli presents his knowledge as a gift, establishing an unequal relationship between the person giving advice and the person whose favour he hopes to win.

characters.name: The new prince
characters.body: A ruler who has acquired a state, rather than simply inheriting established authority. Many of the book's hardest problems begin here.

characters.name: The armed prophet
characters.role: An example of power behind reform
characters.body: Machiavelli's category for founders able to enforce a new order. Read it as an argument about institutions and force, not as a single character.

characters.name: Hannibal
characters.body: An ancient general used to examine discipline, fear and the management of an army. Machiavelli contrasts judgments of conduct with political effects.

characters.name: Fortuna
characters.role: Fortune or the power of circumstance
characters.body: A personified idea rather than a historical figure. She gives a name to events that resist calculation and the limits facing political skill.

characters.name: Marcus Aurelius
characters.body: The speaker throughout Meditations, recalling teachers, testing judgments and giving himself instructions. His position grants immense authority over other people, yet his notes return to ordinary difficulties such as irritation, vanity and reluctance to work. Read the repeated reminders as evidence of a continuing practice.

characters.name: Epictetus
characters.role: The Stoic teacher Marcus encountered through books
characters.body: A formerly enslaved philosopher whose teaching strongly influenced Marcus. He stressed the importance of distinguishing our judgments and choices from what lies beyond our control. Marcus did not need to meet him to become his student: the surviving teachings gave him arguments to practise.

characters.name: Antoninus Pius
characters.body: The emperor under whom Marcus prepared for rule. In Book 1, Marcus recalls qualities he admired in him, including steadiness, patience and attention to public responsibilities. These memories make virtue concrete, locating it in habits the younger man had watched someone practise.

characters.name: Junius Rusticus
characters.role: A teacher who directed Marcus towards philosophy
characters.body: Marcus credits him with correcting his vanity and introducing him to the teachings of Epictetus.

characters.name: Diognetus
characters.body: Remembered for encouraging a serious interest in philosophy and a less credulous approach to superficial enthusiasms.

characters.name: Logos
characters.role: Reason and the order of the whole
characters.body: A central Stoic idea, not a character. Marcus links the rational order of nature with human capacities for judgment and cooperation.

characters.name: Gabriel John Utterson
characters.body: Reserved, loyal and slow to condemn, Utterson is accustomed to keeping other people's affairs private. A disturbing story about Edward Hyde and an unusual clause in Jekyll's will draw him into an inquiry. His concern for his friend has to contend with his reluctance to intrude.

characters.name: Dr. Henry Jekyll
characters.role: A respected doctor with private concerns
characters.body: Prosperous and well regarded, Jekyll belongs to Utterson's circle of old friends. His connection with Edward Hyde is difficult for them to understand. As questions gather around his affairs, his wish to be left alone makes their attempts to help increasingly uneasy.

characters.name: Edward Hyde
characters.role: The unsettling stranger in Jekyll's affairs
characters.body: A man whose conduct alarms witnesses and whose appearance leaves them struggling to explain their disgust. He has access to Jekyll's property and a place in his will. Utterson wants to discover what gives this stranger such a hold over his friend.

characters.name: Dr. Hastie Lanyon
characters.body: A doctor with firm views about respectable science. A professional disagreement has opened a distance between him and Jekyll.

characters.name: Richard Enfield
characters.body: A relative and man about town whose account of a disturbing encounter begins Utterson's inquiry.

characters.name: Poole
characters.body: A longstanding servant with a close view of the household's daily routines. Changes inside the house make that knowledge important.

characters.name: Sir Danvers Carew
characters.body: An elderly gentleman and client of Utterson. His name enters the investigation as it moves beyond a private concern.

characters.name: Candide
characters.role: An innocent young man with a reassuring education
characters.body: Raised in a baron's household, Candide has learned to trust his tutor's explanation that everything is arranged for the best. Affectionate and inexperienced, he carries that confidence into a world that gives him little reason to keep it. His hopes survive an astonishing amount of contrary evidence.

characters.name: Pangloss
characters.role: The tutor who can explain everything
characters.body: A philosopher employed in the baron's household, certain that the world forms the best possible arrangement. He is remarkably skilful at fitting experience to that conviction. His pupil's trust makes his confident explanations consequential long after the lesson has ended.

characters.name: Cunégonde
characters.body: The young woman Candide loves and one of the reasons his childhood world seems so desirable. She belongs to a household proud of its rank. The distance between the life imagined for her and the experiences she recounts gives the story another perspective on what survival costs.

characters.name: Cacambo
characters.body: Experienced, practical and quick to understand a new situation. His usefulness often becomes clear while other people are still explaining events.

characters.name: Martin
characters.body: A man whose experience has given him little confidence in human goodness. His arguments challenge Candide from the opposite direction to Pangloss.

characters.name: The old woman
characters.body: A survivor with a long story of her own. She brings practical judgment and a difficult perspective on other people's misfortunes.

characters.name: The young baron
characters.body: Proud of his family's position. Changes in circumstance do little to loosen his attachment to rank.

characters.name: Marcus Brutus
characters.role: A senator divided between friendship and Rome
characters.body: Respected for his integrity and close to Caesar, Brutus is troubled by the possibility that one man's power could overwhelm the republic. He wants his conduct to be governed by honour. That desire makes him both difficult to recruit and vulnerable to arguments about what an honourable man must do.

characters.name: Julius Caesar
characters.body: A victorious general whose prominence excites popular enthusiasm and aristocratic fear. Caesar is attentive to how others see him and impatient with signs of weakness. As the play opens, people around him are debating what his authority means and whether he might accept a crown.

characters.name: Mark Antony
characters.body: A politician and soldier associated with Caesar, apparently more at home in public celebration than Brutus. His loyalties and his ability to read an audience become important to the contest over Rome. Listen for the distance between how others describe him and what his words can accomplish.

characters.name: Cassius
characters.role: A senator intent on resisting Caesar
characters.body: Shrewd, resentful and persuasive. He understands the political value of Brutus's reputation and looks for an argument that will move him.

characters.name: Portia
characters.body: Intelligent and resolute, she asks to be trusted with the concerns her husband is struggling to conceal.

characters.name: Calpurnia
characters.body: Attentive to signs of danger. Her private appeals must compete with the public expectations surrounding her husband.

characters.name: Casca
characters.role: A senator with a sharp tongue
characters.body: Reports public events with sardonic detachment. His account of the crowd and Caesar helps shape what other people believe they have seen.

characters.name: Decius Brutus
characters.body: Distinct from Marcus Brutus. He knows how to make advice appeal to Caesar's pride and public ambitions.

characters.name: Octavius
characters.body: A younger claimant to authority whose relationship with Antony brings another calculation of power into the play.

characters.name: Lepidus
characters.body: Associated with Antony and Octavius in the struggle for control. Others openly assess his usefulness and importance.

characters.name: Cicero
characters.body: A respected name in Roman public life. His presence gives a sense of the wider political world around the central conflict.

characters.name: The soothsayer
characters.body: Addresses Caesar in public with a warning that others must decide how seriously to take.

characters.name: Artemidorus
characters.role: A man trying to reach Caesar
characters.body: Carries urgent information. His effort to be heard exposes the difficulty of getting through the crowd around a powerful man.

characters.name: Lucius
characters.body: Attends Brutus in private, bringing ordinary fatigue and domestic dependence into the world of political deliberation.

characters.name: Cinna the conspirator and Cinna the poet
characters.body: One belongs to the conspiracy; the other is a poet. Keeping them distinct matters when names become politically charged.

characters.name: Jane Eyre
characters.role: The orphan who tells her own story
characters.body: Jane begins as a dependent child, painfully conscious of injustice and hungry for affection. As she grows, she seeks work, friendship and the right to direct her own life. Her voice is passionate, observant and unwilling to accept that having little money should make her feelings count for less.

characters.name: Edward Rochester
characters.body: The owner of the house where Jane becomes a governess. Abrupt, restless and difficult to predict, Rochester takes an unusual interest in her conversation. Their encounters bring questions of trust and equality into a relationship already shaped by his wealth and her dependence on employment.

characters.name: Helen Burns
characters.body: A thoughtful pupil who meets harsh treatment with a patience Jane struggles to understand. Her faith and affection offer Jane another way of responding to injury. Their friendship matters because Jane can love someone whose convictions about forgiveness are so different from her own.

characters.name: Mrs. Reed
characters.body: The mistress of Gateshead, where Jane spends her early childhood. Her authority determines how much belonging Jane is allowed within the household.

characters.name: John Reed
characters.body: A boy who uses the privileges of his position in the family to bully a child with much less protection.

characters.name: Bessie Lee
characters.body: Sometimes stern, sometimes affectionate. Her stories and occasional kindness offer Jane moments of warmth in an unhappy home.

characters.name: Mr. Brocklehurst
characters.body: Preaches humility and discipline for the school's pupils. Jane must learn what his principles mean in practice.

characters.name: Miss Temple
characters.body: A composed and compassionate authority figure. She gives Jane an experience of adult judgment joined to fairness.

characters.name: Mrs. Fairfax
characters.body: Welcomes Jane to her new employment and explains the household's arrangements. She offers company without knowing every aspect of its life.

characters.name: Adèle Varens
characters.body: A lively French girl in Rochester's care. Her lessons give Jane a daily responsibility and a place within Thornfield.

characters.name: Grace Poole
characters.body: A reserved member of the household whose duties are not immediately clear to Jane.

characters.name: Blanche Ingram
characters.body: Beautiful, confident and at ease in wealthy company. Her presence makes differences of rank particularly visible to Jane.

characters.name: Richard Mason
characters.body: A man with a prior connection to Rochester. His arrival raises questions that Jane is not yet able to answer.

characters.name: St. John Rivers
characters.body: Disciplined and ambitious in his religious vocation. His understanding of duty poses questions about the relationship between service and personal desire.

characters.name: Diana Rivers
characters.body: Intelligent and warm, with interests that offer Jane the possibility of a different kind of companionship.

characters.name: Mary Rivers
characters.body: Shares her sister's serious interests and capacity for friendship. Their household offers a new setting for Jane's search for belonging.

characters.name: Bertha Mason
characters.body: Kept in a secluded part of Thornfield under Grace Poole's care. Her existence changes Jane's understanding of the household and of Rochester. Much of what we hear about her comes from other people, making the absence of her own account important to consider.
characters.revealPolicy: After Jane learns her identity and marriage in Chapter 26 of the 38-chapter novel; omit the entire entry, including name, before then.
